title: Check yourself: KISS in concurrent code

questions.stem: Each Account has synchronized deposit(), withdraw() and balance() methods, and transfer(a, b, amount) locks both accounts, lower id first. A nightly report adds up balance() over 10,000 accounts, one after another, while customers keep making transfers. What does the report show?

options.text: The exact total every night, since each balance() it calls holds that account's lock while reading
options.says: each lock protects one account; the sum is a fact about all of them that no single lock protects

options.text: The exact total every night, since transfers take the two account locks in one fixed order
options.says: a fixed lock order prevents deadlock; it does nothing for a reader that takes the locks one at a time

options.text: A total that is sometimes off, since a transfer can run between an account already added and one not yet added
options.says: money moved from an uncounted account into a counted one is missed, and the other way it is counted twice

options.text: A total that is sometimes off, since balance() can read an account while a transfer is half way through changing it
options.says: balance() takes the account's lock, so it never sees one account half changed; the error comes from reading accounts at different moments

origin.section: A Lock per Bin Keeps Every Move Right and Every Total Wrong

questions.stem: A tracker keeps the slowest request time: `long seen = max.get(); while (latency > seen && !max.compareAndSet(seen, latency)) { Thread.onSpinWait(); }`, where max is an AtomicLong holding 10. Two threads record 40 and 70 at the same moment, and the one recording 70 wins. What happens to the thread recording 40?

options.text: It keeps looping until the process ends, since every retry compares against the 10 it read before the loop
options.says: seen is never read again, max never returns to 10, so every compareAndSet fails and the condition stays true

options.text: It keeps looping until the 70 is stored, since compareAndSet waits for a competing write to complete
options.says: compareAndSet never waits: it compares and either sets or fails at once

options.text: It leaves the loop with max at 70, since its compareAndSet fails once another thread has changed the value
options.says: a failed compareAndSet keeps the loop going: the condition is !compareAndSet(...), and latency > seen is still true

options.text: It leaves the loop with max at 40, since its compareAndSet writes 40 over whatever value it finds
options.says: compareAndSet writes only when the current value equals the expected one, and 70 is not 10

origin.section: A compareAndSet Loop That Reads the Value Once Spins Forever; incrementAndGet Leaves No Loop to Get Wrong

questions.stem: settings() runs `if (!ready) { synchronized (this) { if (!ready) { ready = true; settings = fetch(); } } } return settings;`, with ready a volatile boolean. At startup the config server is down, and the first call's fetch() throws. Ten minutes later the server is back. What do calls to settings() get from then on?

options.text: Every call returns null, since ready already says loaded and nothing calls fetch() again
options.says: the flag was set before the fetch; the failure left settings null and ready true, so the check skips the fetch for good

options.text: Every call throws the startup failure, since the exception was kept and is handed to each caller
options.says: nothing stores the exception; later calls skip the block and return the field, which is null

options.text: The next call gets the settings, since it finds the settings field null and calls fetch()
options.says: the check reads ready, not the settings field, and ready is true

options.text: The next call gets the settings, since the volatile flag makes it check again inside the lock
options.says: volatile makes the write of true visible; the check inside the lock reads that same true and skips the fetch

origin.section: A Double-Checked Flag Can Say Loaded Before the Value Is; a synchronized Getter Can't

questions.stem: A ticketing service gives its seats one owner thread and publishes an immutable snapshot after every change. hold(n) runs on the customer's thread: if snapshot().free() >= n it submits a task that subtracts n from the free seats, otherwise it refuses. Four seats are free when two customers each ask for three, while the owner is still busy with an earlier task. What happens?

options.text: One hold goes through and one is refused, since the owner runs the two submitted tasks one after the other
options.says: the tasks only subtract; running them one after the other doesn't refuse anything, because the decision was made before

options.text: One hold goes through and one is refused, since the second customer's snapshot already includes the first hold
options.says: a snapshot changes only after the owner applies a task, and the owner hasn't run either one yet

options.text: Both holds go through and free seats reach -2, since both customers checked the same snapshot before either task ran
options.says: the check and the change are on different threads; both checks saw 4 free, and the owner then subtracted 3 twice

options.text: Both holds go through and free seats reach -2, since the owner thread runs the two submitted tasks at the same time
options.says: a single-thread executor runs one task at a time; the problem is that the tasks don't check

origin.section: One Lock Makes the Total Right; One Owner Thread Also Keeps Readers From Waiting
